title: Unit 4 Review — Choosing the Right Tool

phase1.explanation:
Two very different rooms in the workshop, and both boil down to the same skill: [[key:picking the right tool for a job you can actually describe]], not memorizing every method on every class.

[[term:For storage]], the questions that actually matter: Do I need order? (List, yes — Set/Map, no guarantee unless it's a Tree variant). Do I need to block duplicates? (Set or Map's keys — never List). Do I look things up by position, or by a label? (List's get(index) vs. Map's get(key)). Do I need it sorted at all times, or is sorting-on-demand fine? (TreeSet/TreeMap's O(log n) cost vs. a HashSet/HashMap plus one sort when you actually need order). Do I only ever touch the ends? (Deque, not a general List).

[[term:For concurrency]], the questions shift: Am I sharing mutable state between threads at all? If not, none of this unit's synchronization machinery is even needed. If yes — is the danger a race condition on a single value (synchronized is usually enough) or genuine coordination between threads, like a producer waiting on a consumer (wait()/notify())? And [[warn:am I about to hand-roll new Thread() for every task, or is this actually a job for an ExecutorService pool]] — almost always the pool, once there's more than a couple of short-lived tasks involved.

[[fun:the throughline across all fifteen lessons]]: every tool in this unit is a trade-off someone already thought through — speed against order, flexibility against safety, simplicity against control. [[key:knowing the trade-off is the actual skill]] — the specific method names are just vocabulary for expressing a decision you already know how to make.
phase1.openingDialogue: Unit 4 complete! You've mastered collections and threads! 🎉

phase2.explanation:
Conceptual review — no broken code!

Common misconception: "I should always use the most generic interface (List, Set, Map) everywhere."

Actually: Use the most specific interface that meets your needs. This makes your code more expressive and prevents unnecessary restrictions.

Example:
• If you need FIFO, use Queue (not List)
• If you need unique elements, use Set (not List)
• If you need sorted keys, use TreeMap (not HashMap)

Another misconception: "synchronized is too slow, I should avoid it."

Actually: Synchronization is necessary for shared mutable state. Avoid it by:
• Using immutable objects
• Using thread-safe collections
• Using atomic variables

Only synchronize when you need to!

phase3.openingDialogue: Final check! Can you choose the right tool? 🧰

mcq.question:
You're building a student management system. You need:
1. Fast lookup of students by ID
2. No duplicate student entries
3. Students should be sorted by name for printing

Which collection should you use?

A) ArrayList with manual sorting
B) HashSet
C) TreeSet
D) HashMap
E) TreeMap

Select the BEST combination.

phase5.trivia: The java.util.concurrent package — Executors, Future, and everything else this unit's second half touched — shipped in the same Java 5 release (2004) as generics, which is why this unit's two halves (Generics in 4.6, concurrency in 4.10–4.14) share a birthday in Java's own history, even though they don't feel related on the surface.
